For g(h)=sigmoid(Wh+2)/sigmoid(2), W=0 gives g=1: the gate initially preserves whatever it multiplies. Direct calculation gives range (0,1.1353) and initial derivative with respect to its logit of 1−sigmoid(2)=0.1192. Thus amplification is limited to about 13.5%, while suppression can approach zero. Both sigmoid tails saturate, weakening gate learning; bias 2 already reduces sensitivity relative to logit zero. Initially, the gate’s input Jacobian is zero because W=0, although W can receive gradients. In y=x+g(h)⊙F(x), initialization reproduces the ordinary residual block x+F(x), rather than making the whole block identity. Closing the gate suppresses the residual update while leaving x untouched.

[Highway Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00387) use y=H(x)⊙T(x)+x⊙(1−T(x)); negative transform-gate biases favor carrying inputs initially. Unlike an unchanged identity skip, their coupled carry gate directly controls input retention. [ReZero](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v161/bachlechner21a/bachlechner21a.pdf) uses x+αF(x), α initialized to zero, producing an exact initial identity map and initial dynamical isometry. Residual-branch parameter gradients initially vanish until α moves away from zero.

[LayerScale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.17239) learns per-channel residual scales initialized to small positive values, allowing residual contributions to develop progressively; its unconstrained scales avoid sigmoid saturation. These papers support residual scaling as an optimization mechanism, not evidence of historical forgetting. For the proposed gate, an unchanged skip preserves a direct information route, but does not guarantee recoverability after residual cancellation or downstream processing. Gate magnitudes alone cannot establish that older interactions were forgotten; controlled history perturbations are needed.
